House Democrats begin leadership elections, Jeffries poised to clinch speaker nomination
Today, House Democrats are set to begin their closed-door leadership elections. One particular race to watch: minority leader Hakeem Jeffries is expected to seek the caucus’ formal backing as its candidate for Speaker in the next Congress through a recorded vote, according to several reports.
Jeffries is widely expected to win and, with Democrats poised to hold a sizeable House majority, secure a glide path to the speakership when the full chamber votes in January. If elected Speaker, Jeffries would become the first Black person to hold the gavel in US history.
Jeffries is not facing a challenger, and despite the possibility of some defections from the incoming progressives, he is still expected to have the 218 votes needed to win on the House floor.
Democrats will cast votes for House majority leader and whip, and the caucus chair and vice chair, among other positions.
The DealBook summit, an annual conference hosted by the New York Times that brings together business leaders, lawmakers and officials is taking place today.
It’s a packed agenda with Canadian prime minister Mark Carney, SpaceX and Tesla founder Elon Musk, and Zohran Mamdani, the New York mayor, all set to take the stage.
The Times just noted that vice-president JD Vance has canceled his appearance at the conference, citing a series of scheduled meetings that have been planned to address the myriad tech outages that have plagued banks, the airline industry and tech companies in recent days.
Doctors and public health leaders expressed grief and alarm at the loss of US measles-free status, a hard-won public health victory that once made the US a leader in infectious disease elimination.
Measles was declared resurgent in the United States, Bolivia and Mexico by the Pan American Health Organization (Paho) on Tuesday, meaning the virus has spread continuously for 12 months.
The announcement formally ends a 26-year record of measles elimination in the US, and comes amid the worst measles outbreak since 1991, making the loss of measles elimination status widely predicted. The Americas were once the only measles-free World Health Organization (WHO) region on the globe.
“There’s no question it was emotional, because we’ve been working on this initiative for decades,” said Dr Jon Andrus, the chair of the Paho advisory committee that recommended the US lose its measles elimination status.
“To see the US, once a global leader, lose its status is of course sad,” Andrus continued, citing the work of friends and colleagues, “and it was also sad to see our Mexican colleagues lose their status, as well as Bolivia.”
That grief was in sharp contrast to the reaction of the Trump administration. Health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has spent years spreading misinformation about the measles, mumps and rubella combination vaccine (MMR) and downplaying the disease, had his agency promote an appearance with a Texas-based chef and posted a picture of himself as James Bond this week. After devastating midterm losses, Trump appointed Maha advocate Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff.
The US is in the midst of the worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 5,400 cases and 10 measles-associated deaths reported by state health authorities. Measles is considered one of the most infectious diseases known to medicine. The infection kills one to three unvaccinated people per 1,000 and hospitalizes up to one in five.

Top oversight Democrat sends letters to Trump allies and aides: ‘This is just the beginning’
Congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chair of the House oversight committee, has sent 12 letters to members of Donald Trump’s family, current and former officials, and aides urging them to preserve documents ahead of the sweeping inquiries that Democrats are set to launch in the new Congress.
The document retention letters, were addressed to vice-president JD Vance, Eric Trump, Donald Trump Jr, Stephen Miller, the White House chief of staff, and his predecessor, Susie Wiles, among others. Garcia noted that the scope of the likely investigations will focus on alleged family corruption, misconduct at the Department of Homeland Security, and the justice department’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files.
“Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this Administration’s self-dealing, misconduct, and abuse,” Garcia said in a statement. “These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans. This is just the beginning.”
My colleagues are covering the latest from Shenzen, China, at our dedicated live blog. This includes the sidebar between Canadian prime minister MarkCarney and Donald Trump at the summit.
Carneys office issued a statement following the meeting, noting that “the leaders discussed the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement that would create good jobs, boost affordability, and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture, and sovereignty. They agreed to continue the work and to stay in close contact.”
The Chinese, US and Russian leaders exchanged first greetings in China, a day before their first formal trilateral meeting.
Footage showed Russian leader Vladimir Putin shaking hands with Donald Trump and the two exchanging pleasantries with China’s Xi Jinping before taking their positions for a group photo at an Apec summit in Shenzhen.
Mullin heads to Congress to face questions over flight disruptions, football trip and immigration
Homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin is set to appear today at a congressional hearing about threats facing the country.
His appearance comes at a time of looming questions over cyber infrastructure, the future of immigration enforcement and his decision to fly to the LSU-Texas college football game as travellers across the US were stuck at airports after the nationwide grounding of flights.
The hearing in front of the House homeland security committee is a standard yearly opportunity for members of Congress to grill top administration officials over national security threats.
The hearing is also the first opportunity for Democrats after their midterm defeat of Republicans to grill the cabinet official who is key to president Donald Trump’s mass deportation agenda.
Two others expected to face lamwakers are FBI deputy director Christopher Raia and the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton.
Late into the night on 3 November, while the lower 48 states were reeling from the blue wave crashing across the US, Mary Peltola took to the stage in a Sheraton hotel ballroom in Anchorage, Alaska, to greet her supporters.
It wasn’t a victory speech as such – there would still be long days ahead before all votes could be counted across this vast arctic state. But that didn’t prevent the Democratic Senatecandidate from expressing her elation, bouncing up and down on stage, clapping her hands and clicking her fingers.
Before she could speak, a volunteer shouted out from the back of the hall: “Aarigaa!” Peltola picked up the refrain, and threw it right back:
“Aarigaa! Can we just chant aarigaa? Aarigaa! Aarigaa!”
It was just one word. But it encapsulated something special about Peltola and her insurgent’s campaign to unseat the incumbent Republican US senator, Dan Sullivan.
“Aarigaa” is an Iñupiaq word that is commonly understood across Alaska’s 229 federally recognised tribes. It is a word of celebration, of relief almost, that roughly translates to: “Way to go!” or “Attaboy!”
Now, Peltola genuinely has a reason for exclaiming it. On Tuesday – two weeks after the midterm elections – the tortuous count was finally completed, and she was declared winner.
In prevailing, she becomes the first Alaska Native to take a seat in the US Senate.
Mary Peltola’s win in Alaska to give the Democrats a commanding Senate majority of 56-44 seats has been hailed as “a gift” by the party’s leader.
Peltola will be Alaska’s next senator after beating the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, with the result called two weeks on from midterm elections which saw Donald Trump’s party lose ground across the country.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, who enlisted Peltola to challenge Sullivan, wrote on social media that her victory is a “gift to Alaska, the Senate, and all of America”.
“It’s official: 56 Democratic Senate seats!” Schumer added. “Her knowledge and love for Alaska are unparalleled, and she ran a pitch-perfect campaign devoted to the issues Alaskans care most about – fish, family, and freedom.”
Peltola, a former US House lawmaker, is the first Democrat the state has elected to the Senate since 2008. Her victory comes just two years after Alaska voters unseated her while supporting Trump by a double-digit margin.
“From Juneau to Utqiagvik, the message from Alaskans is clear: the status quo in DC is not working for Alaska,” Peltola said in a statement on Tuesday.
“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,” she said. “As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska’s working families.”
However, Peltola’s success has not been without controversy. Last month the New York Times reported that her staffers were involved in a scheme to recruit another Republican challenger, also named Dan Sullivan, to appear on the ballot.
Peltola’s campaign had denied any involvement in encouraging the second Sullivan’s run, and after state election officials tried to remove him, Alaska’s supreme court in June ruled he be allowed to appear on the ballot.
Trump called for Peltola to be prosecuted over the apparent ruse, and Alaska’s top federal prosecutor announced that criminal and civil inquiries were under way, while the state’s governor separately announced plans to open a criminal investigation.

In other developments:
The National Security Agency’s internal network, NSANet, went down on Tuesday. An NSA spokesperson said the outage was the resulted of “scheduled routine maintenance”. Speaking in Manila, Donald Trump brushed off the news saying: “It’s like when you’re big and powerful, and you have all the money. Things like that happen. It’s fine.” Secretary of state Marco Rubio said there is “no evidence” that any of the many outages this week “are related to each other” or “nefarious actors” and director of national intelligence Jay Clayton said the outages are likely due to system upgrades and not a cyber-attack.
The White House has dropped its nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration. Overton faced a challenging path to Senate confirmation, particularly after Republican senator Bill Cassidy said that he remained undecided about her nomination ahead of a Senate health, labor and pensions committee vote scheduled for Wednesday.
Chuck Schumer again insisted that he has the votes to secure the leadership position when Democrats take the majority in the Senate in the new year. “We are all united together,” Schumer said, despite the fact that several members of the caucus have pledged support for senator Chris Van Hollen.
Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, saidhe is making “a nice ask” for an additional $50bn in funding for air safety upgrades following the nationwide ground-stop of thousands of flights last week. Duffy also said the FBI is now assisting the investigation into the newly installed router responsible for the grounding.
Hung Cao, who currently serves as the acting navy secretary, faced lawmakers on the Senate armed services committee to be confirmed as the branch’s permanent top official. During his hearing, Cao said the eight suicide attempts on board the USS Abraham Lincoln – during a record-breaking deployment– were actually “suicide mitigations”, and defended conditions on the warship.
Jensen Huang, the embattled former CEO of Nvidia, will appear before House lawmakers on three key committees on 1 December. The chair of the company’s board has said Nvidia “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”.
After the United States lost its measles elimination status, which it achieved in 2000, health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, a longtime vaccine skeptic, blamed “worldwide COVID-era disruptions” for interrupting routine childhood vaccination.
Trump was granted a temporary delay before he must give a witness statement in his $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC. A federal district court judge extended the deadline for Trump to sit for a deposition by the UK broadcaster’s lawyers from 11 December until 22 January.
